name: Oxlint (oxc-project/oxc)
workload: Linting the VS Code, Vue core, and Sentry codebases (standard + type-aware rule sets) cold, no incremental cache
claimed_speedup: 50-100x faster than ESLint depending on CPU cores (up to ~118x on M4 Max, ~62x on M2 Max multi-core); ~2-3x faster than Biome
hardware: MacBook Pro M2 Max (12-core); MacBook Pro M4 Max 64GB; MacBook Air M3 24GB 8-core
tradeoffs: Oxlint implements a subset of ESLint's rule set (no plugin ecosystem parity yet); type-aware linting benchmark excludes rules requiring full type info to keep comparison fair, which understates ESLint+typescript-eslint's real-world cost but also means Oxlint's rule coverage is narrower.
caveats: Benchmark is run and published by the Oxc project itself (not fully independent); hyperfine output shown but exact ESLint/Oxlint version pins and full command lines for each run are not reproduced in the README excerpt read this session, only the summary hyperfine blocks. Compiler flags not applicable (installed as prebuilt Rust binaries via npm).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than eslint" -> oxc-project/bench-linter

name: Ruff
baseline: Flake8 (linting); Black (formatting); also compared to pycodestyle, pyflakes, pylint
workload: Linting/formatting the CPython codebase from scratch, plus incremental single-file re-lint
claimed_speedup: 10-100x faster than existing linters (Flake8) and formatters (Black); founder's blog post: ~150x faster than Flake8 on macOS (~25x if Flake8 multiprocessing is hacked on), ~75x faster than pycodestyle, ~50x faster than pyflakes and pylint; incremental single-file re-lint of CPython ~60ms
stars_or_usage: 49.8k stars; used in Apache Airflow, Apache Superset, FastAPI, Hugging Face Transformers, Pandas, SciPy
tradeoffs: Not 100% rule-for-rule identical to Flake8/Black in every edge case (docs claim near-total parity); newer/smaller plugin ecosystem than the tools it replaces.
caveats: No hardware/CPU model stated for the headline numbers; the founder's blog post (pre-Astral, written by the original creator) is the most detailed public source but is still a first-party account, not an independently reproducible benchmark harness. The repo's own criterion benchmarks (crates/ruff_benchmark) measure Ruff internals only, not a head-to-head run against Flake8/Black.
found_via: GitHub: known project, cross-checked via gh api repos/astral-sh/ruff and its README-linked founding blog post

name: Biome
workload: Cold formatting/linting of a real JS/TS project tree (webpack-scale corpus) with all files already correctly formatted, using hyperfine
claimed_speedup: Formatting: ~25x faster than Prettier, ~20x faster than parallel-prettier/xargs -P, 1.5-2x faster than dprint, single-threaded ~7x faster than Prettier (up to ~100x multithreaded on an M1 Max 10-core). Linting: ~15x faster than ESLint (no plugins), single-threaded ~4x faster.
hardware: MacBook Pro 13-inch, M1, 2020 (also notes an M1 Max 10-core run for the 100x figure)
tradeoffs: Linting comparison only enables rules both tools support and excludes type-aware rules (favors Biome, which lacks type-aware linting); Biome does not support incremental/cached formatting the way Prettier and dprint do, so the cold-format comparison is the favorable case for Biome.
caveats: The benchmark/ directory (bench.js + Dockerfile + README with these numbers) was removed from the repo's main branch in commit 8e4ada5 ("chore: remove benchmark from repository", #10355); numbers above are read from the last commit before removal (fdf8555f) and are no longer linked from the current biomejs.dev homepage benchmark link, which now 404s. Treat as a historical, project-authored benchmark rather than a currently maintained one.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/biomejs/biome/commits?path=benchmark, then reading benchmark/README.md at commit fdf8555f; also biomejs.dev homepage "~35x Faster than Prettier ... Intel Core i7 1270P" claim

name: ty
workload: Cold CLI type-check of home-assistant/core (no cache); incremental re-check latency in the language server after editing one file in pytorch/pytorch
claimed_speedup: Cold CLI check on home-assistant/core: ty 2.19s vs Pyrefly 5.32s vs Pyright 19.62s vs mypy 45.66s (ty ~9x faster than Pyright, ~21x faster than mypy; derived from page data). LSP incremental re-check on pytorch/pytorch: ty 4.5ms vs Pyright 370.5ms vs Pyrefly 2.60s (ty ~82x faster than Pyright, ~578x faster than Pyrefly; derived from page data). README headline: "10x-100x faster than mypy and Pyright."
tradeoffs: ty is still in beta with an unstable API and incomplete type-system coverage vs. mature mypy/Pyright; only mypy supports warm/cached re-checks in this benchmark, so the cold-check comparison favors checkers with fast cold starts.
caveats: Benchmark is designed and run by the ty team, i.e. by the project being evaluated, comparing itself favorably to competitors including another project in this same batch (Pyrefly) - not an independent third party. However the harness (astral-sh/ruff/scripts/ty_benchmark) is public and reproducible, and states tool versions (latest of each) and hardware (M4), which is why it is rated A rather than C.
found_via: GitHub: discovered via astral-sh org (same org as Ruff/Oxlint search trail); gh api repos/astral-sh/ty and astral.sh/blog/ty benchmark chart, methodology at github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/scripts/ty_benchmark/README.md

name: Pyrefly
workload: First-party: type-checking PyTorch. Third-party reproducible check: cold CLI type-check of home-assistant/core on Apple M4 (astral ty_benchmark harness)
claimed_speedup: README: checks >1.85M LOC/sec, type-checks PyTorch ~15x faster than mypy and Pyright (no stated methodology). Independently measured by astral's public ty_benchmark script on home-assistant/core: Pyrefly 5.32s vs Pyright 19.62s vs mypy 45.66s (Pyrefly ~3.7x faster than Pyright, ~8.6x faster than mypy there; derived from page data) - notably slower than that same benchmark's LSP incremental re-check case, where Pyrefly (2.60s) trailed both ty and Pyright.
stars_or_usage: 7.0k stars; default type checker for Meta's Instagram codebase (~20M LOC), adopted by PyTorch and JAX
tradeoffs: Pyrefly's own PyTorch-based "15x faster" headline is unverified in this session (no hardware/methodology found); the corroborating cold-check numbers (~3.7-8.6x vs Pyright/mypy) are smaller than that headline, and Pyrefly's LSP incremental re-check was the slowest of the three checkers in the same harness, so speedup is workload-dependent.
caveats: The Tier A evidence used here (astral's ty_benchmark) was produced by a competing project (Astral/ty), not Pyrefly's own team or a neutral third party, though the code and hardware are public per the rule that "who ran it does not matter" for Tier A. Pyrefly's own README claim ("15x on PyTorch") could not be traced to a page with stated hardware/methodology this session and would only support Tier C on its own.
found_via: GitHub: cross-referenced from the ty benchmark chart (astral.sh/blog/ty) which names Pyrefly as a comparator; gh api repos/facebook/pyrefly

name: clangd-tidy
workload: Running the same clang-tidy checks over a C/C++ codebase: clangd-tidy wraps clangd (which only builds an AST per translation unit and reuses its background index) instead of invoking standalone clang-tidy (which re-parses all included headers, with warnings from them suppressed by default)
claimed_speedup: "clangd-tidy is significantly faster than clang-tidy (over 10x in my experience)"
tradeoffs: No --fix support; silently disables checks clangd doesn't support; some diagnostic behavior differs from clang-tidy (tracked as known discrepancies in the project's issue tracker); requires clangd installed and configured, and a working compile_commands.json.
caveats: "Over 10x" is stated as the author's personal experience with no benchmark script, codebase, compiler flags, or hardware given - capped at Tier C despite the plausible-sounding number. Referenced StackOverflow/community discussion in the README is anecdotal, not a reproducible benchmark.
